deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is a 1805 draft sheet ('Litt. D'). The previous page treats comet orbit relations, and the next page reduces solar positions for the comet of 1772. This page breaks off into trigonometric interpolation, which is the material of Gauss's 'Theoria interpolationis methodo nova tractata' (c. 1805, published posthumously in Werke III). It ends with two parallax-reduction expressions.

(1) Kernel identity. For integer mu >= 1:
 (cos mu t - cos mu a)/(cos t - cos a) = [2 cos(mu-1)t sin a + 2 cos(mu-2)t sin 2a + ... + 2 cos t sin(mu-1)a + sin mu a] / sin a.
Both sides are polynomials of degree mu-1 in cos t.

(2) Value at the node. For t = a the left side becomes, by l'Hopital in the variable cos t, (mu sin mu t / sin t) at t = a, i.e. mu sin mu a / sin a. Gauss states this.

(3) Interpolation formula. The nodes x = a, b, c, d, ... are the mu values a + 2 pi j/mu ('a complete period'). They are exactly the roots in cos x of cos mu x = cos mu a. Lagrange's basis function for node a is
 L_a(t) = sin a (cos mu t - cos mu a) / [mu sin mu a (cos t - cos a)].
It equals 1 at t = a and 0 at the other nodes. Since sin mu b = sin mu a for every node (my remark), the factor 1/(mu sin mu a) is common to all nodes. Expanding with (1) gives
 X(t) = (sin mu a/(mu sin mu a)) (A+B+C+...) [= (1/mu) Sum A]
 + (2/(mu sin mu a)) (A sin(mu-1)a + B sin(mu-1)b + ...) cos t
 + (2/(mu sin mu a)) (A sin(mu-2)a + ...) cos 2t + ...
This is a cosine polynomial of degree mu-1 through the mu data points. The page breaks off in the third line. In modern form, the coefficient of cos jt is (2/mu) Sum_k A_k (cos j x_k - cot(mu a) sin j x_k).

(4) Companion identity, after Gauss crossed out mistaken 'sin a' factors:
 sin t (cos mu t - cos mu a)/(cos t - cos a) = sin mu t + 2 sin(mu-1)t cos a + 2 sin(mu-2)t cos 2a + ... + 2 sin t cos(mu-1)a.
This is the sine analogue, needed for sine terms.

(5) Aliasing reduction. 'In a function consisting only of cosines', on the node set cos mu x = cos mu a, one may replace
 cos lambda x = [sin(l mu a) cos(lambda - k mu)x - sin(k mu a) cos(lambda - l mu)x] / sin((l-k) mu a).
More generally, if lambda = lambda' = lambda'' mod mu, then
 0 = sin(lambda'-lambda'')a cos lambda x + sin(lambda''-lambda)a cos lambda' x + sin(lambda-lambda')a cos lambda'' x
holds at every node.
- Proof (mine): write x = +-a + 2 pi j/mu and lambda = r + n mu. Then cos lambda x = cos(lambda a +- r*2 pi j/mu), with the same phase phi for all three terms. The claim reduces to sin(B-C)cos(A+phi) + sin(C-A)cos(B+phi) + sin(A-B)cos(C+phi) = 0. This holds because sin(B-C)e^{iA} + sin(C-A)e^{iB} + sin(A-B)e^{iC} = 0.
- Consequence: as a polynomial in cos x, the expression is divisible by cos mu x - cos mu a.
- The first formula is the special case lambda' = lambda - k mu, lambda'' = lambda - l mu.
- Gauss then states the mu = 1 form. For arbitrary integers k, k', k'', both sin(k'-k'')a cos kx + sin(k''-k)a cos k'x + sin(k-k')a cos k''x and the same with sin kx etc. are divisible by cos x - cos a. They vanish at x = +-a; the sine version is sin x times a polynomial in cos x that vanishes at cos a.

(6) Parallax reduction (unrelated block). Two model expressions are written, with the quantities l, lambda, E, b and the latitude-rate letter underlined, possibly marking unknowns:
- Longitude: l + lambda(theta - E) + pi{cos phi cos(theta+L) sin(l + lambda(theta-E)) - cos eps cos phi sin(theta+L) cos(l + lambda(theta-E)) - sin eps sin phi cos(l + lambda theta - lambda E)}.
- Latitude: b + beta(theta - E) + pi{sin eps cos phi sin(theta+L) - cos eps sin phi}.
Interpretation (mine):
- The body moves linearly in longitude and latitude from epoch E.
- pi is the horizontal parallax, phi the observer's geographic latitude, eps the obliquity, and theta+L the local sidereal angle.
- The observer's unit vector (cos phi cos(theta+L), cos phi sin(theta+L), sin phi) is rotated to ecliptic coordinates: X = cos phi cos s, Y = cos eps cos phi sin s + sin eps sin phi, Z = -sin eps cos phi sin s + cos eps sin phi, with s = theta+L.
- The braces are X sin l - Y cos l (first-order parallax in longitude, with the 1/cos b factor dropped) and -Z (parallax in latitude for b about 0).
- Hence these are observation equations corrected for geocentric parallax, plausibly for least-squares fitting of a short arc.
errors: No substantive mathematical error found in the identities.
In the companion sine identity Gauss first wrote spurious factors 'sin a' (by analogy with the first identity) and struck them out; the corrected version is right.
The constant term sin mu a/(mu sin mu a) is left unsimplified (= 1/mu).

The interpolation formula relies tacitly on sin mu b = sin mu a for all nodes, which holds only for nodes a + 2 pi j/mu (the 'complete period' hypothesis); the omitted denominators sin b, sin c, ... are absorbed correctly in that case. The third line is unfinished.

The aliasing rule and its general form hold only on the node set cos mu x = cos mu a, i.e. modulo cos mu x - cos mu a, not identically; Gauss signals this with 'in einer Function ... kann man statt ... setzen'.

Parallax expressions: the longitude term lacks the 1/cos b factor and the latitude term keeps only the b=0 part, so they are first-order approximations for a body near the ecliptic. Acceptable but approximate.

results.what: (cos mu t - cos mu a)/(cos t - cos a) expanded as a finite cosine sum, plus its sine companion
results.modern_name: Chebyshev-type difference quotient / Dirichlet-like kernel for trigonometric Lagrange interpolation
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Euler/Lagrange-era trigonometric identities); used systematically in Gauss's Theoria interpolationis

results.what: Cosine-polynomial interpolation through mu equally spaced nodes a + 2 pi j/mu, with explicit coefficients
results.modern_name: Trigonometric (Lagrange) interpolation / discrete cosine-type transform on a shifted equispaced grid
results.usually_credited_to: Clairaut, Lagrange (1750s-60s); Gauss, Theoria interpolationis methodo nova tractata (c.1805, publ. 1866)

results.what: On the node set cos mu x = cos mu a, frequencies congruent mod mu are linearly dependent via sin(lambda'-lambda'')a cos lambda x + cyclic = 0; divisibility by cos x - cos a
results.modern_name: Aliasing of frequencies on a discrete grid
results.usually_credited_to: Implicit in Gauss's Theoria interpolationis; modern aliasing concept (Nyquist, 20th c.)

results.what: Geocentric parallax corrections in ecliptic longitude and latitude for a body moving linearly in time
results.modern_name: Parallax reduction (equatorial-to-ecliptic rotation of the observer's geocentric vector)

deep.surprise_reason: The material belongs to Gauss's 1805 work on trigonometric interpolation (Theoria interpolationis, Werke III), whose content including aliasing-type relations is known and credited to him. The page is a draft of known work. The parallax formulas are routine.

transcription_corrections: Line 4: 'Ebenso[?] also die Formel' — the first word is uncertain in the image (possibly 'Erhält'/'Ebenso'); sense: 'thus the formula by which X=A,B,C,... for x=a,b,c,... is represented, when these values form a complete period'.
Second identity: Gauss struck out 'sin a' after sin mu t and after 2 sin(mu-1)t; the corrected text is sin mu t + 2 sin(mu-1)t cos a + 2 sin(mu-2)t cos 2a + ... + 2 sin t cos(mu-1)a.
In the last line, the underlined coefficient before (theta - E) is probably a distinct letter for the latitude rate (beta / a script B), not the epoch symbol E as transcribed.
In the first line the crossed-out text before (mu-1)a is a false start; read 2 cos t sin(mu-1)a + sin mu a.
